title: Remember 9/11. Remember Who We Were on 9/12.
author: The Ways of a Gentleman
source: The Ways of a Gentleman (Substack), September 11, 2026
summary: This essay uses the memory of national unity after September 11, 2001 as the occasion for a practical argument about civil discourse and personal deportment in disagreement. Its central claim is that the post-9/11 solidarity Americans remember was not accidental but behavioral, produced by specific habits of listening and self-restraint that have since atrophied, and that individuals can choose to practice again regardless of the broader political climate. The piece lays out a sequence of interpersonal disciplines: listening to understand rather than to rebut, disagreeing without personal insult, entertaining the possibility that one is wrong, staying composed when provoked, and disengaging from arguments that serve no purpose. Its recurring move is to treat 'deportment' — how a person behaves specifically under provocation or disagreement — as the real test of character, framing civility not as softness but as a disciplined leadership skill that individuals control even when others do not reciprocate it.
points: The essay argues that post-9/11 national unity was produced by specific behaviors (listening, restraint, checking on neighbors) rather than being an automatic byproduct of tragedy, implying those behaviors can be deliberately revived.
It distinguishes listening to understand from listening merely to find an opening to rebut, arguing the latter has become the online default.
It explicitly separates disagreement from disrespect, arguing that ad hominem attacks typically signal a lack of substantive argument rather than strength.
'Deportment' is defined as how a person behaves specifically when insulted or provoked, not when agreed with, and is proposed as the real measure of character.
The piece frames intellectual humility, including the willingness to say 'I was wrong,' as a mark of maturity rather than weakness.
quotes: Political divisions didn't disappear completely, but for a little while they didn't seem important. Americans checked on their neighbors and strangers comforted each other. Flags appeared on homes and businesses across the country.

Too often, we don't listen in order to understand anymore. We listen for the opening we need to attack. Sometimes we don't even do that. We see a few words on a screen and immediately start writing our response.

You can express a strong opinion without cursing at someone. You can challenge an argument without calling the person making it an idiot. You can defend your principles without questioning someone's intelligence or character.

This is where deportment matters. How we carry ourselves when someone agrees with us tells us very little about our character. How we carry ourselves when someone insults us or says something we find offensive tells us a lot more.
Intellectual humility also requires us to extend to others the possibility we instinctively grant ourselves, that they may have arrived at their beliefs sincerely and for reasons they consider sound.
Humility isn't weakness. The ability to say, "I hadn't thought about it that way," or even, "I was wrong," is a true mark of maturity.
